Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: What is the worst mistake Ukraine is making against Russia?
Answer: I usually refrain from criticizing the way Ukraine conducts the war. After all, they are doing the dying while the rest of us is comfortable and safe. However, after my friends and I have recently been targeted by Russian forces and have suffered casualties, I’ll make a small exception: Ukraine is losing too many soldiers. I never understood this quasi-obsession with keeping control over as much territory as possible. Ukraine has enough land but not enough soldiers. Interestingly, whenever Ukraine is forced to abandon its static defense, they prove to be more successful. A good example is Russia’s recent Kharkiv offensive. Ukrainian defense positions near the border with Russia weren't properly prepared (and sometimes didn't exist at all) which forced the Armed Forces of Ukraine to withdraw to more defensible positions. In other words, they gave up land for tactical gains. This wasn't voluntary (as we all know) but it has proven to be the right step. Now Russian troops get slaughtered in Vovshansk and other Ukrainian border towns by the thousands. A cemetery in Ukraine. (Picture by the author of this post) Ukraine needs to exploit its strengths and not allow the Russians to dictate how the game is played. As soon as troops are moving (in one or the other direction), Ukraine is at an advantage (due to more mobility, better leadership, logistics, and coordination). On the other hand, as soon as all movements stop and attrition warfare begins, they are losing valuable resources. We need to be more modest with our expectations. Ukraine keeping its losses at a sustainable level while at the same time making the Russians bleed should be the absolute top priority. Question: How can a person find out if a soldier has been killed in the war in Ukraine?
Answer: If you are a family member, you can ask the unit he or she was serving with for information. Every soldier in the Armed Forces of Ukraine has to fill in an emergency contact list with the contact details of his or her next of kin. This means that close family members (spouse/parents) are usually the first to learn about a soldier’s fate. If you’re a friend of this soldier, you can ask them. The Western embassies in Kyiv are usually less forthcoming with information. They won't confirm to a stranger that a certain person is dead or missing. Ukrainian soldiers with the coffin of a former U.S. Army soldier who was killed in Ukraine. (Picture: Yevhenii Zavhorodnii) Then there are social media channels and accounts. When a soldier dies, his comrades often publish posts about it. The media also regularly report about soldiers who were killed on the battlefield. In this case, Google is your friend. Last but not least, if everything else fails, there are Russian Telegram channels such as “Track a nazi merc” that publish information about the fate of Western volunteers fighting in Ukraine. I would be careful with their “info”, though. Their sources aren't reliable and it happened several times they declared a soldier to be dead only to retract their statements later. Question: How is it to live in Ukraine right now? Do the civilians prepare for war or do they live like normal?
Answer: Some people prepare, others don’t. There are guys who bought themselves a rifle (mostly AR-15 variants) and train at the shooting range three times a week. A few of them even take lessons in infantry tactics from army instructors. Some people also have stockpiled food at home. Then there are others who (try to) pretend that the war is far away and can’t touch them. These are often rich folks who flock to the fancy bars every weekend while the rest of the population saves some money to give to the military. At the shooting range. Some of my coworkers in Ukraine are gun owners and also take shooting lessons. I’ve seen the same happening in other wars. During my time in Kosovo, I met some civilian refugees who brought everything with them you need to survive for many weeks in the forest. On the other hand, other folks didn't even carry a water bottle and were dressed as if they wanted to visit a nightclub. Name: Roland Bartetzko
Question: How does the density of mining in Ukraine compare to previous combat actions?
Answer: Before I came to Ukraine, I fought in two wars, Bosnia and Kosovo. I also worked as a deminer after the war in Kosovo. In every aspect of this issue (number of mines, density of minefields, number of booby traps, and unexploded devices), Ukraine is worse than what I’ve ever seen before. I just returned from a trip to the warzones in the East of the country and the minefields the Russians have left there often stretch for many kilometers. We drove on roads where the area on both sides was off-limit. A house in a village to the northeast of Kharkiv. (Picture by the author of this post) In addition, some villages are completely mine-infested. Instead of walking or driving around, you need a drone to assess the situation. This is especially bad for civilian refugees who want to return to their homes. They cannot even enter their houses until those are cleared. The operations to demine these areas will probably take many years. People in countries such as Bosnia or Croatia and even Cambodia still get killed by landmines although the fighting there ended many years ago.
